{{Short description|1959 philosophical paper by J. R. Lucas}}
"'''Minds, Machines and Gödel'''" is [[John Lucas (philosopher)|J. R. Lucas]]'s 1959 philosophical paper in which he argues that a human [[mathematician]] cannot be accurately represented by an [[Turing machine|algorithmic automaton]]. Appealing to [[Gödel's incompleteness theorem]], he argues that for any such automaton, there would be some mathematical formula which it could not prove, but which the human mathematician could both see, and show, to be true.

The paper is a [[Gödelian argument]] against [[Mechanism (philosophy)|mechanism]].

Lucas presented the paper in 1959 to the [[Oxford Philosophical Society]]. It was first printed in ''Philosophy'', XXXVI, 1961,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lucas |first1=J. R. |author-link=John Lucas (philosopher) |title=Minds, Machines and Gödel |journal=Philosophy |date=1961 |volume=36 |issue=137 |pages=112–127 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/3749270 |url-access=registration}}</ref> then reprinted in ''The Modeling of Mind'', [[Kenneth M. Sayre]] and Frederick J. Crosson, eds., Notre Dame Press, 1963, and in ''Minds and Machines'', ed. Alan Ross Anderson, Prentice-Hall, 1964, {{ISBN|0-13-583393-0}}.
